results.title: Cursor is coming for GitHub. It's called Origin. But this isn't just ... - Instagram
results.content:
Cursor is coming for GitHub.  
  
It’s called Origin.  
  
But this isn’t just another GitHub alternative.  
  
Cursor is building a new Git forge for a world where AI agents are writing, reviewing, and shipping a huge amount of the code.  
  
Traditional Git platforms were designed around humans:  
  
Write code → create PR → review → merge.  
  
But when hundreds of AI agents can work on different tasks simultaneously, that workflow starts to look very different.  
  
That’s where Origin comes in.  
  
It’s designed around agent-driven development, with code hosting, review, and collaboration built for this new way of working.  
  
And this is a much bigger move for Cursor than it initially looks.  
  
Cursor started with the editor.  
  
Then came agents. [...] Cursor started with the editor.  
  
Then came agents.  
  
Now it’s moving into where the code itself lives.  
  
If AI agents become the primary producers of software, the infrastructure managing all that code becomes incredibly valuable.  
  
Origin is currently waitlist-only, with Cursor saying it will be available in fall 2026.  
  
The bigger question:  
  
If Cursor can own the editor, the agents AND the code repository, how much of the software development stack can it eventually control?

The former GitHub CEO just raised $60M to rebuild developer tooling for the agentic era. He might be right that git needs a rethink — I've been hacking around the same problems.

Thomas Dohmke left GitHub and launched Entire, a developer platform built from scratch for the age of AI coding agents. It’s the largest seed round in dev tools history.

results.title: Forge | Andrew Nesbitt
results.content:
Git forges are the same kind of problem. GitHub has `gh`, GitLab has `glab`, Bitbucket has various unofficial options, and Gitea/Forgejo has `tea`. They all manage repos, issues, pull requests, releases, and CI, with completely different syntax, different flag conventions, and different ideas about which API endpoints deserve a command and which don’t.

I’ve been building something that needs to talk to all of these forges, a project I’m not quite ready to announce yet, and the idea of wrapping four different CLIs with four different output formats and four different authentication flows was not appealing. I wanted one interface that worked the same way everywhere, for humans on the command line and for AI coding agents that need to interact with forges programmatically. [...] I suspect more people than usual are going to need something like this soon. AI coding agents are starting to interact with forges directly, opening issues and creating pull requests and triggering CI, and most of them are hardcoded to GitHub’s API. Having a single interface that works the same way against a Forgejo instance as it does against github.com makes the agent code simpler and the forge choice less of a lock-in decision.
